items.prompt: What is a role definition?
choices: The posting text used to attract applicants to it
A written list of what this job needs, shown as tasks
A job title combined with its salary band and reporting line
items.explanation: It is the list of requirements, written as things a candidate can show.

items.prompt: Which of these is a checkable signal?
choices: Seems like a natural problem solver to most people
Gives off calm, positive energy in every conversation
Diagnoses an incident from logs
items.explanation: A signal names something observable on a task. The others are impressions.

items.prompt: Why does 'good judgment' fail as a requirement?
choices: Nobody can say what a candidate must do to show it
It is too rare a quality for any hiring loop to find
It matters only in roles that manage other people
items.explanation: Without a visible behaviour there is nothing to score.

items.prompt: A resume line says 'led incident response.' What is it?
choices: A signal, since it appears in writing
A claim that still needs a task to confirm it
Proof, because the employer already verified it
items.explanation: Claims become evidence only when a task confirms them.

items.prompt: When is the role definition written?
choices: After the team has chosen a final candidate
At the debrief
Before the first interview is scheduled
items.explanation: The loop is designed from the definition, so it must exist first.

items.prompt: What should a signal let an interviewer do?
choices: Score what they saw
Record how much they liked the candidate overall
Compare the candidate against their own career path
items.explanation: A signal turns observation into a score.

items.prompt: Which restates 'good communicator' checkably?
choices: Speaks fluently and keeps eye contact
Explains a trade-off so a stakeholder can decide
Answers every question quickly without hesitating
items.explanation: The restated version has a task and an outcome that can be judged.

items.prompt: How many signals did the scenario's role definition hold?
choices: Two signals
Five signals in all
Three signals
items.explanation: Incident diagnosis, stakeholder trade-offs and code review.

items.prompt: A manager lists 'strong ownership' as a requirement. Which rewrite makes it usable in a loop?
choices: Shows ownership in how they talk about their previous team and its goals
Stays with an employer for several years without moving on
Describes following a problem past their own part, and what they did
Gives confident answers about owning outcomes in general terms
items.explanation: Only the first names a behaviour a candidate can describe and an interviewer can score. The others still reward how the candidate sounds or how long they stayed.
items.reference:
Vague trait vs. signal
❌ "Seems smart" — no task, no pass or fail
✅ Diagnoses an incident from partial logs
❌ "Good communicator" — rated by feel
✅ Explains a trade-off so a stakeholder can decide
Why: a requirement only helps a loop if someone could fail it on a specific task.
items.learnMore:
Role definition and signals

A role definition lists what this job needs as things a candidate can demonstrate. Each item is a signal: observable, scoreable, tied to a task.

Common mistake

Treating a resume claim as a signal. It is an assertion that still needs a task to confirm it.
items.reflection: Think of a role you have worked in. Which of its requirements could you have turned into a task someone could watch?

items.prompt: Role definition X says 'smart, driven, great fit.' Y lists incident diagnosis, trade-off explanation and code-review focus. What does Y allow that X does not?
choices: Hiring faster, since fewer items means fewer interviews
Skipping the debrief, because the signals already decide the outcome
Designing one slot for each requirement and scoring each
Guaranteeing the chosen candidate will succeed in the role later
items.explanation: Y gives each slot something to look for. It does not remove the debrief or guarantee outcomes.

items.prompt: What is the halo effect?
choices: Rating every candidate highly because the team is short-staffed
Favouring candidates who resemble the interviewer
One visible strong trait lifting ratings of unobserved traits
items.explanation: The key is a single trait spreading to others.

items.prompt: Which trait creates the halo in the scenario?
choices: The candidate's confident, articulate manner
The candidate's three-month record on the job
The role's written list of signals
items.explanation: The manner was on display in the one exercise that ran.

items.prompt: Does the halo effect need careless interviewers?
choices: Yes, only careless or poorly trained interviewers ever fall for it
No, honest interviewers can be shaped by real feelings
Yes, it needs a deliberate bias
items.explanation: It operates on sincere impressions.

items.prompt: Which skill did the halo cover for in the scenario?
choices: Stakeholder communication
Rapport
Incident diagnosis
items.explanation: The unobserved skill borrowed credit from the observed one.

items.prompt: Is confidence in a candidate a bad sign?
choices: No, it is real information about what it was measured on
Yes, confident candidates usually hide weak skills behind it
Yes, it should be marked down
items.explanation: The error is using it as a stand-in for other things.

items.prompt: What is the best structural defence?
choices: Telling interviewers to be more careful and watchful
One signal per slot, scored before discussion
Adding extra open conversations to the loop
items.explanation: Structure limits what a vivid trait can spread to.

items.prompt: 'Everyone loved them' reliably tells you...
choices: That every required skill was demonstrated in the loop
That the role was well defined
How the candidate came across to people present
items.explanation: Liking is evidence about impression only.

items.prompt: A rave from the one exercise that ran says nothing about...
choices: The signals whose exercises were cut
The signal that exercise was designed to target
Whether the candidate attended
items.explanation: It speaks to what was observed, not to what was not.

items.prompt: A rapport chat, a communication exercise and the hiring manager all say 'strong.' Where does a halo most plausibly show up?
choices: The communication exercise scoring a skill it tested directly
The debrief being held after the interviews had finished
The role listing three signals
The chat and manager rating depth they never saw
items.explanation: The halo is where unobserved traits get rated. The exercise did observe its signal.
items.reference:
One trait, many ratings
😃 Visible: confident, articulate
👀 Observed: stakeholder communication only
❓ Never seen: incident diagnosis, code review
➡️ Rated 'strong overall' anyway
Why: a vivid trait colours our rating of things we never watched.
items.learnMore:
The halo effect

One salient positive trait raises how we rate unrelated traits. It works through honest feelings, so trying harder does not remove it; structure does.

Common mistake

Treating it as carelessness. Careful, well-meaning interviewers are affected too.
items.reflection: When did a first impression of someone make you assume things about them you had not actually checked?

items.prompt: Which change reduces halo the most?
choices: Adding a fourth open conversation with a more experienced leader
Asking interviewers how impressed they felt, out of ten
Letting the most enthusiastic interviewer speak first
Each interviewer writes a score on their signal before any debrief
items.explanation: Independent written scores on a specific signal limit spread. More impression-gathering feeds it.

items.prompt: A candidate is awkward in conversation but excels at the diagnosis exercise. What is the halo-type risk?
choices: None, since quiet candidates cannot create a halo effect
Only the diagnosis score matters, so conversation can be ignored
A negative impression cannot spread once an exercise ran
Poor conversation ratings dragging the diagnosis score down
items.explanation: The effect works in both directions: a weak visible trait can drag other ratings down.

items.prompt: Five interviewers agree after open chats. How many independent observations?
choices: About one, repeated
Five, one from each person
None, because chats cannot be counted
items.explanation: They reacted to the same visible trait.

items.prompt: What makes evidence independent?
choices: Each observer holds the same job title
Each observer looked at something different
Each observer reached the same score
items.explanation: Independence is about distinct things observed.

items.prompt: When should interviewers record their scores?
choices: After the loudest view is heard
Whenever the debrief ends
Before any discussion has started
items.explanation: Writing first keeps views from converging.

items.prompt: Why was the bake-off judges' agreement weak?
choices: All five reacted to the decoration, not the taste
Five judges is too few for a fair contest to be run
The cake was too good to compare
items.explanation: They agreed about the same surface feature.

items.prompt: What happens if the most enthusiastic person speaks first?
choices: Their view is discounted by the group
Later speakers tend to adjust toward them
Everyone becomes more independent in response
items.explanation: First speakers anchor the discussion.

items.prompt: One observation of the right thing vs. several impressions of the wrong thing?
choices: Several impressions outweigh a single observation
They are exactly equal in value
The single observation carries more
items.explanation: Relevance beats count.

items.prompt: A written score should record...
choices: What the interviewer saw on their signal
How much they enjoyed the whole hour with them
A ranking of the others
items.explanation: The record should be tied to an observation.

items.prompt: Does adding interviewers always add evidence?
choices: Yes, every extra person always adds a fresh observation
No, only if each looks at something different
Yes, up to five people
items.explanation: Duplicated looks add little.

items.prompt: Panel A: four open chats, all say 'strong.' Panel B: three people on different signals score 4, 2 and 5 out of 5. Which tells you more about fit?
choices: B, because three separate looks show strengths and a weak spot
A, because four people agreeing is stronger than three scores
A, because open chats cover more ground than fixed exercises
B, because lower scores are always more trustworthy than high ones
items.explanation: B's scores rest on separate observations and reveal a weak spot. A's agreement rests on a shared impression.
items.reference:
Counting observations
💬 4 open chats, all 'strong' → 1 trait, counted 4 times
🧪 3 separate exercises → 3 observations
✍️ Score in writing first, then talk
Why: agreement is as strong as the number of different things looked at.
items.learnMore:
Independent evidence

Evidence is independent when each observer looked at something different and recorded it before hearing others. Otherwise agreement mostly reflects a shared reaction.

Common mistake

Counting heads. Five agreeing opinions about the same impression are one data point.
items.reflection: Think of a group decision you were part of. Did people look at different things, or react to the same one?

items.prompt: The debrief opens with the hiring manager sharing excitement. What is the best fix?
choices: Collect written scores first, then discuss
Ask the manager to skip the debrief entirely this time
Have interviewers wait until the end to form any view
Switch to a vote once the discussion has finished
items.explanation: Written, prior scores keep independent observations from being pulled together. Voting after discussion keeps the anchor.

items.prompt: Two interviewers both ran a 'tell me your career story' chat and agreed. How much does their agreement add?
choices: Little, since both saw the same thing in similar ways
Double, since two people confirmed the story independently
Nothing, because repeated agreement is always worthless
More than one exercise, since there are more words
items.explanation: Two looks at one thing add little, though not literally nothing.

items.prompt: What does a slot need first?
choices: A list of every trait the role needs
One signal to look for
A friendly interviewer who has free time
items.explanation: One slot, one signal.

items.prompt: What is the 'task' of a slot?
choices: What the interviewer hopes to feel afterward
What the candidate says about their past work
What the candidate actually does during it
items.explanation: The task creates the observation.

items.prompt: Why write the bar for a yes in advance?
choices: So scoring does not bend to mood
So candidates can prepare polished model answers
So the debrief can be skipped
items.explanation: A pre-set bar fixes what counts.

items.prompt: Which comes first?
choices: Designing the slots first, then deciding what they should test
Deciding what the job needs, then designing slots
Scheduling interviewers, then the role
items.explanation: The definition drives the loop.

items.prompt: Is a rapport chat allowed in a structured loop?
choices: No, any unscored slot defeats the loop
Yes, and it counts toward every signal
Yes, if it is not counted as evidence on the signals
items.explanation: It has a legitimate job as long as its limits are respected.

items.prompt: A slot is assigned 'judgment' with no task. It will likely become...
choices: An open chat scored by impression
A rigorous exercise with a clear bar and scorer
A slot nobody bothers to run at all
items.explanation: Without a task or bar, impression fills the gap.

items.prompt: Who scores a slot?
choices: The whole panel by show of hands
That slot's interviewer, in writing
The candidate afterwards
items.explanation: The person who watched records it.

items.prompt: Which part is the 'bar'?
choices: The total time allowed for the slot, set by the schedule
The room
What a yes looks like, written beforehand
items.explanation: The bar is the scoring standard.

items.prompt: The signal is 'explains a trade-off to a non-technical stakeholder.' Which slot design is complete?
choices: Chat about communication style and judge it afterward
Explain a trade-off to a mock stakeholder, with a written bar and scorer
Present past projects while the panel votes on who spoke best
Explain anything at all, then score how confident and fluent the candidate seemed
items.explanation: Only the first has task, written bar and scorer. The others score impression.
items.reference:
Parts of a slot
🎯 Signal — what single thing is it looking for?
🛠️ Task — what does the candidate actually do?
📏 Bar — what a yes looks like, written in advance
✍️ Scorer — who records it, before what
Why: a slot missing any part slides back into an open chat.
items.learnMore:
From signal to slot

Each slot needs a signal, a task, a written bar and a scorer. The role definition comes first and the slots are designed from it, not the reverse.

Common mistake

Designing the loop first and writing the definition to match.
items.reflection: Pick a skill you want to check in someone. What task would make it visible, and what would a pass look like?

items.prompt: A team designs five open chats first, then writes a role definition to match. What is the likely result?
choices: A tighter match to the job's real needs, since both were aligned later
Slots test whatever interviewers find easy to ask
More independent evidence than a loop designed from the definition
No difference, since the order of the two steps does not matter
items.explanation: The definition has to come first to drive the slots.

choices: Subtract points from every signal score
Note it as comfort information, not as a signal score
Reject the candidate, since rapport predicts every skill
Re-run the chat until it goes well
items.explanation: Letting an unscored slot leak into scored signals brings back the halo.

items.prompt: How many signals did the scenario require?
choices: Two signals
Four required signals
Three signals
items.explanation: Incident diagnosis, stakeholder trade-offs and code review.

items.prompt: How many signal exercises actually ran?
choices: One of the three
Two of the three
All three
items.explanation: Only stakeholder communication ran.

items.prompt: Which exercise ran?
choices: Incident diagnosis from partial logs
Stakeholder communication
Code review
items.explanation: The candidate's strongest area.

items.prompt: How many signals were left untested?
choices: One
Three
Two
items.explanation: Signals 1 and 3 had no exercise.

items.prompt: Why was the surviving rave misleading?
choices: It measured one signal yet was read as a whole verdict
It was scored by an unqualified interviewer in a hurry
It came from the final debrief
items.explanation: One observation was stretched over all three signals.

items.prompt: If all three signal slots were cut, how many signals are untested?
choices: Two of them
All three
Only one
items.explanation: One slot per signal means three cuts remove all three.

items.prompt: What was the debrief like in the scenario?
choices: Written scores against each signal, shared first
Skipped entirely by the manager
Informal, with impressions instead of scores
items.explanation: There were no per-signal scores to compare.

items.prompt: The cuts hid the loss because...
choices: 'We've seen enough' did not name the signal lost
The role definition had never been written down
The candidate hid the weakness on purpose
items.explanation: A vague reason hides which signal went.

items.prompt: Five steps were planned and steps 2 and 4 were cut. Which statement is exact?
choices: Signal 1 was tested lightly in the rapport chat
Signals 2 and 3 had no evidence at all, while signal 1 was tested well
Signals 1 and 3 had no evidence; signal 2 had a strong score
All three signals had partial evidence from the debrief
items.explanation: Steps 2 and 4 held signals 1 and 3. Step 3 ran. The chat and informal debrief gave no per-signal scores.
items.reference:
The scenario's loop
1 Rapport chat — ran, unscored on signals
2 Incident diagnosis — cut
3 Stakeholder trade-offs — ran, strong
4 Code review — cut
5 Debrief — informal
Why: two cut signal slots left two of three signals with no designed exercise.
items.learnMore:
Reading a loop slot by slot

Laying planned against actual slots shows exactly which signals have evidence. With one slot per signal, each cut removes one signal.

Common mistake

Reading the loop as one overall impression instead of a signal-by-signal table.
items.reflection: Think of a plan that got trimmed under time pressure. What exactly did the trimming remove, and did anyone say so?

items.prompt: Suppose each signal had two slots and one slot per signal was cut. How does that compare with the one-slot design where three cuts leave all three untested?
choices: Each signal is still wholly untested, as before
All three signals become untested, exactly as they did in the one-slot design
Each signal keeps one slot, so none is wholly untested
It depends on how the interviewers feel on the day
items.explanation: Redundant slots mean a cut thins evidence without erasing it, at the price of more time.

items.explanation: The score was accurate for its own signal. The harm came from stretching it.

items.prompt: Which is an honest response to time pressure?
choices: Cutting a slot and naming the gap
Cutting slots and saying nothing
Running the loop without scoring
items.explanation: Honesty means the loss is visible.

items.prompt: Which is a falsifiable debrief observation?
choices: Seemed great overall, and everyone on the panel enjoyed talking with them
Picked the likeliest cause, could not say why others fit worse
Gave me a good feeling
items.explanation: It can be checked against what happened.

items.prompt: Does catching a gap force a different hiring decision?
choices: Yes, the candidate is always rejected afterward
No, since gaps never matter in practice
Not necessarily; the team may hire with a plan
items.explanation: The value is informed choice.

items.prompt: What is the loop's main value?
choices: The decision rests on what was observed
Every hire it approves will succeed on the job
Shorter hiring
items.explanation: Evidence under the decision, not guaranteed results.

items.prompt: Does this idea apply beyond hiring?
choices: No, only to interviews for engineering roles
Yes, to any panel such as a promotion committee
Only to decisions made by one person alone
items.explanation: Any panel can double-count a shared impression.

items.prompt: What does a different role such as a technical writer need?
choices: The same three signals reused unchanged
No written signals
Its own specific signal list
items.explanation: Signals belong to a role.

items.prompt: Why revisit a role definition over time?
choices: Real needs shift as the team changes
Candidates ask to see it
Interviewers forget what it says by the end of each quarter
items.explanation: A stale list tests what used to matter.

items.prompt: Treating the loop as bureaucracy gets what wrong?
choices: It adds interviews and paperwork that nobody really needs
It is risk management for gaps like the scenario's
It needs managers
items.explanation: It exists to catch the unobserved.

items.prompt: A time-pressed manager must drop one of three signal slots. What is the best move?
choices: Drop whichever slot is hardest to schedule for the panel
Drop the signal where the candidate already seemed strongest
Drop none, but skip the written scoring to save time
Drop the signal with least day-to-day weight, name the gap, plan onboarding
items.explanation: A deliberate, named cut on the least critical signal keeps the trade-off visible.
items.reference:
Three responses to time pressure
🕒 Keep all slots, shorter — thinner scores, nothing unseen
✂️ Cut one on purpose, name the gap — plan around it
🤐 Cut and say nothing — gap discovered on the job
Why: the loop's value is what the decision rests on, not a different outcome.
items.learnMore:
What the decision rests on

A structured loop does not promise a different hire. It makes the decision rest on observed evidence, with gaps named and planned for.

Common mistake

Judging the loop by whether it changed the offer.
items.reflection: Pick a decision you made recently. What did it rest on: something you observed, or a general impression?

Candidates will refuse offers for lack of detail
The debrief will run longer than the interviews do, wasting the day
The loop tests what used to matter and misses on-call skills
items.explanation: Roles change, so definitions need review.
